catalog_quote: [p. 96, §3.7.1] Stress is not distinctive in Yawuru, at least in the sense that no pairs of words are distinguished on the basis of different stress positions with otherwise identical sequences of segmental phonemes. Stress in Yawuru, however, is not completely predictable, either. [§3.7.1.1 Primary stress] In the majority of words, primary stress (indicated by the acute accent mark) is assigned to the first syllable, regardless of the number of syllables or moras that make up the word. [fn. 130, p. 97] Currently on record are 2 words with primary stress on the 2nd syllable, 15 words on the 3rd, 6 words on the 4th, and 3 words on the 5th. These constitute only a very small percentage of general lexicon. A count based on a working vocabulary of 1730 nominals indicates that 1704 words (or over 98%) have their primary stress on the 1st syllable. Onomatopoeic items, interjections and verb roots are excluded from this count. Compound nouns and proper nouns (such as personal names and toponyms) are included. [p. 98, §3.7.1.2] i) The 1st mora bears primary stress and the 3rd mora, if vocalic, bears secondary stress. ii) If the 3rd mora is a non-vocalic sonorant, then the vowel in the 4th mora takes up secondary stress, unless it is the word-final vowel. [p. 104, §3.7.1.5] The primary stress always falls on the first-order prefix. Regardless of the number of prefixes added to the verb root, the root-initial syllable bears a secondary stress. Verbal suffixes do not bear stress.
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the word (over 98% of nominals), irrespective of word length or syllable weight. Stress is not contrastive, but it is lexically irregular in a small residue: a few dozen compounds, place names, onomatopoeic items and a handful of monomorphemic words carry primary stress on a later syllable, and interjections/onomatopoeics often show final stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Described at length (pp. 98-102): words of more than three syllables usually carry a secondary stress placed by mora counting, where preconsonantal sonorant codas count as moras: "i) The 1st mora bears primary stress and the 3rd mora, if vocalic, bears secondary stress. ii) If the 3rd mora is a non-vocalic sonorant, then the vowel in the 4th mora takes up secondary stress, unless it is the word-final vowel." In reduplicated words secondary stress falls on the first vowel of the repeated half regardless of mora count (p. 102, §3.7.1.4); stress in conjugated verbs is treated separately (§3.7.1.5, not read here).
new_statements.exceptions: Fn. 130: 2 words with primary stress on the 2nd syllable, 15 on the 3rd, 6 on the 4th, 8 on the 5th (mostly suspected compounds, toponyms, e.g. birdirlngaba, kabanyanya; a few monomorphemic words, e.g. dyararu 'spring country', bambida 'small dragon lizard'); interjections and onomatopoeics often word-final (kwala, wardaw); two bound forms with final stress (-nyarra, -aw). "Except for the onomatopoeic items.. no phonological reason is found for the irregular stress distribution."
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms from a dictionary count of 1730 nominals; verb roots, interjections and onomatopoeics excluded from the count; stress in conjugated verbs handled in a separate subsection.
new_statements.identity_note: Hosokawa describes Yawuru of the Broome area, West Kimberley, from work with the last fluent speakers in the 1980s; this is the language-level yawu1244 itself, no dialect split at issue. Glottolog 5.3 lists the language as extinct/reawakening.

new_statements.quote: §3.7.1.5 (p. 104): "Verbs are conjugated by prefixes and suffixes added to a root (see Chapter 4 for details). The primary stress always falls on the first-order prefix. Regardless of the number of prefixes added to the verb root, the root-initial syllable bears a secondary stress. Verbal suffixes do not bear stress. [...] The only exception to the pattern described above is the verb rba 'follow, track'. In this case, the vowel immediately preceding the root (i.e. the final vowel of the prefix complex) bears the secondary stress." §3.7.1.3 (p. 101): "In compound words, the first syllable of the non-initial lexical component usually bears the secondary stress, although it may bear the primary stress in some cases (3.7.1.1). [...] the position of the secondary stress of a Yawuru word is hard to predict without morphological and/or etymological information."
new_statements.citation: Hosokawa, Komei. 1991. §3.7.1.5 'Stress in conjugated verbs' and §3.7.1.3, pp. 99-101 (pp. 131-133) of the same thesis.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's fixed: initial syllable placement (initial stress) and with the existing_statement from §3.7.1.1 of the same thesis; adds that the initial-primary rule extends to conjugated verbs (primary on the first-order prefix, never on suffixes) and to suffixed and compound words, and adds the morphologically conditioned secondary-stress rules and the single verbal exception rba. It does not change the type or the placement of primary stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is on the first syllable of the word: in conjugated verbs it always falls on the first-order (outermost) prefix, however many prefixes precede the root, and verbal suffixes never carry stress; in polymorphemic nominals and toponyms the first syllable of the word keeps primary stress while secondary stress goes to the first syllable of the (first) suffix or of the non-initial compound member. This is the same first-syllable placement already recorded from §3.7.1.1 (pp. 96-97), now shown to hold for verbs and derived/compounded words too.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Verbs (p. 104): the root-initial syllable bears secondary stress regardless of the number of prefixes (yáabìlka, íngarrabìlkanda, wánggarrabìlka); in reduplicated verbs the repeated root also takes secondary stress (ínabìlkabìlkanda). Polymorphemic words (p. 101): first syllable of the (first) suffix takes secondary stress whatever its mora count (dyíru-ngànydyal 3rd mora.. kárrambal-ngànydyal 6th mora); in compounds the first syllable of the non-initial component usually takes secondary stress; the non-initial syllables of the first component never do. Monomorphemic words (pp. 98-101, Table 314): mora-counting, 1st mora primary, 3rd mora secondary if vocalic, else the 4th-mora vowel unless word-final; word-final open syllable on an odd mora may be half-lengthened (optional). Reduplicated words (pp. 102-103): secondary stress on the first vowel of the repeated half, promoted leftwards when the repeated half begins with w-, y-, r- (elders) — younger speakers reinterpret (wúmangu-màngu).
new_statements.exceptions: Verbs: the sole exception is the monosyllabic CCV root rba 'follow, track', whose secondary stress falls on the last prefix vowel (ínàrbanda); reduplicated bulibuli 'bathe' and rbarba take secondary stress on only the first half of the repeated root (ngábùlibulinda, ínàrbarbarn). Polymorphemic words: compounds may put the primary stress on the non-initial component 'in some cases' (cross-ref. §3.7.1.1, p. 97: 26 of 1730 nominals with non-initial primary stress, mostly suspected compounds, two apparently monomorphemic dyarúru, bambída, plus onomatopoeia/interjections with final stress); toponyms and a few nominals (bidyára 'ear', kúyarabí 'cocky apple', dyinyírri 'very hot') show irregular secondary-stress placement (p. 102). Secondary-stress position 'is hard to predict without morphological and/or etymological information' (pp. 101-102).
new_statements.identity_note: The thesis describes Yawuru of the Broome area, West Kimberley (title page, p. 2), i.e. yawu1244 / ISO ywr; §3.7.1.4 (2) notes a sociolectal difference in secondary-stress placement in reduplicated words (elders vs young speakers), not a dialect split. No other variety is described in the sections read.
